concepts.name: Python function
concepts.definition: A named block of code defined with def that takes inputs and can return a value. Prerequisite: lesson 13 reviews it.

concepts.name: Python dict
concepts.definition: A collection of key-value pairs; you look a value up by its key. Prerequisite: lesson 12 reviews it.
concepts.analogy: A phone's contact list: look up a name, get the number.

concepts.name: Python list
concepts.definition: An ordered collection of values you can index, loop over and change. Prerequisite: lesson 12 reviews it.

concepts.name: Python tuple
concepts.definition: A fixed, ordered group of values, often used to return two things at once. Prerequisite: lesson 12 reviews it.

concepts.name: Python if statement
concepts.definition: Runs a block of code only when a condition is true, with elif and else for other cases. Prerequisite: lesson 12 reviews it.

concepts.name: Python string methods
concepts.definition: Built-in methods on text, such as startswith, lower and split. Prerequisite: lesson 12 reviews it.

concepts.name: Python for loop
concepts.definition: Runs a block once for each item in a list, dict or other collection. Prerequisite: lesson 12 reviews it.

concepts.name: Python f-string
concepts.definition: A string with f before the quotes that fills in {expressions}, like f"Saved {name}". Prerequisite: lesson 12 reviews it.

concepts.name: Python import
concepts.definition: Brings in a module so its code can be used, like import os or import json. Prerequisite: lesson 18 reviews it.

concepts.name: Python core types
concepts.definition: int, float, str and bool, and converting between them with int(), str() and bool(). Prerequisite: lesson 12 reviews it.

concepts.name: Backend
concepts.definition: The part of an app that runs on computers the company controls: it takes requests, checks them, stores and fetches data, and sends back answers.
concepts.analogy: The restaurant's staff: the server (the waiter) who takes and checks your order, and the kitchen behind the swinging doors.

concepts.name: Frontend
concepts.definition: The part of an app the user sees and touches: pages, buttons and layout, running on the user's own device.
concepts.analogy: The dining room: the tables, the decor, everything the customer sees.

concepts.name: Never trust the client
concepts.definition: The client is whatever sends the request; for users, that's a device they control, so they can change or skip anything there. The backend checks every request itself.
concepts.analogy: A customer can ask for anything; the server still checks the order before the kitchen cooks.

concepts.name: IP address
concepts.definition: The number computers use to find each other on a network: four numbers for IPv4, a longer form with colons for IPv6.
concepts.analogy: The restaurant's street address.

concepts.name: DNS
concepts.definition: The Domain Name System: turns a name like pokeapi.co into an IP address. A resolver finds the answer, and the resolver, computer and browser each cache it for a while.
concepts.analogy: Looking up a restaurant's street address when you only know its name.

concepts.name: TCP
concepts.definition: Runs on top of IP and gives a reliable, ordered conversation: it numbers the data, re-sends what's missing and puts it back in order. Starts with a three-step handshake.
concepts.analogy: The greeting at the door: You: "Table for one?" Staff: "Yes, we have one. Ready?" You: "Ready." Nobody takes your order before you're seated.

concepts.name: TLS
concepts.definition: Makes a connection private (encrypted) and proves the server's identity with a certificate signed by a certificate authority the browser trusts. Others can still see which site you're visiting, but not what you send. A certificate proves the name, not that the site is honest.
concepts.analogy: A private booth so nobody overhears your order, plus the licence on the wall proving it's the real restaurant.

concepts.name: HTTPS
concepts.definition: HTTP sent through TLS: private, and the server has proved who it is. Plain http:// has neither.
concepts.analogy: Placing your order from the private booth of the licensed restaurant.

concepts.name: Client
concepts.definition: Anything that sends a request: a browser, a phone app, a script, or another server.
concepts.analogy: The customer.

concepts.name: Server
concepts.definition: A program that waits for requests and answers each one: it checks the order, gets what it needs from the database, and sends a response. Also the computer it runs on.
concepts.analogy: The server (the waiter): takes the order, checks it, carries it to the kitchen, brings the plate back.

concepts.name: Database
concepts.definition: Where data is stored so it survives restarts and can be searched. Only the server talks to it.
concepts.analogy: The kitchen: where the food is stored and prepared; customers never walk in.

concepts.name: API
concepts.definition: The list of requests a server accepts and how to make them; on a web API, each item is a method and a path.
concepts.analogy: The menu: what you're allowed to order, and how to ask.

concepts.name: Cache
concepts.definition: Saved copies of recent answers, kept so they can be handed out again without redoing the work (e.g. asking the database).
concepts.analogy: Food made ahead and kept warm under a heat lamp, ready before anyone orders it.

concepts.name: HTTP request
concepts.definition: A message a client sends to a server: a method, a path, headers, and sometimes a body.
concepts.analogy: The order ticket the customer hands the server.

concepts.name: HTTP response
concepts.definition: The server's answer: a status code, headers, and usually a body.
concepts.analogy: The plate brought back to the table.

concepts.name: Status code
concepts.definition: A three-digit number saying how a request went: 2xx went well, 4xx is the client's mistake, 5xx is the server's.
concepts.analogy: "Here you go" (200), "We're out of that" (404), "The order was filled in wrong" (400/422), "Something went wrong on the restaurant's side" (500).

concepts.name: JSON
concepts.definition: A text format for data that any language can read and write; it looks like a Python dict but is a string until parsed.
concepts.analogy: A standard order form any restaurant can read.

concepts.name: HTTP method
concepts.definition: The part of a request saying what kind of action it is: GET reads, POST creates; PUT, PATCH and DELETE change or remove.
concepts.analogy: "Can I see the specials?" is a GET (just looking); "I'd like the pasta" is a POST (it creates an order).

concepts.name: Latency
concepts.definition: The time from starting a request (the click) until the response arrives; every hop adds some.
concepts.analogy: The clock starts when you walk in and stops when the plate lands on your table.

concepts.name: SQL query
concepts.definition: A request written in SQL, the database's own language. The server writes it, the database runs it, and rows come back.
concepts.analogy: The server's note to the kitchen, in the kitchen's own shorthand.

concepts.name: Request journey
concepts.definition: The hops one request takes: DNS lookup, TCP connection, TLS handshake, HTTP request, the server's checks, the database query, and the response back.
concepts.analogy: The whole visit: look up the address, get greeted at the door, sit in the private booth, order, the server checks the ticket, the kitchen cooks, the plate comes back.

concepts.name: Shell
concepts.definition: The program inside a terminal that reads your commands and runs them. Ubuntu's is bash.

concepts.name: Command, options and arguments
concepts.definition: A command line is the command (what to do), options or flags starting with - (how to do it), and arguments (what to do it to), e.g. ls -l poketeam.

concepts.name: Working directory
concepts.definition: The folder the shell is in right now; pwd shows it and cd changes it. Relative paths start from here.
concepts.analogy: The "You are here" dot on a mall map.

concepts.name: Absolute path
concepts.definition: A path starting with /, the top of the file system, so it means the same place wherever you are.
concepts.analogy: Directions from the mall's main entrance: they work wherever you are.

concepts.name: Relative path
concepts.definition: A path that starts from the working directory; . is the current folder and .. the one above.
concepts.analogy: Directions from the "You are here" dot; .. is "back out to the corridor".

concepts.name: Hidden file
concepts.definition: A file whose name starts with a dot, like .env; plain ls leaves it out and ls -a shows it.

concepts.name: File permissions
concepts.definition: Read, write and execute rights for a file's owner, its group and everyone else, shown by ls -l and changed with chmod.
concepts.analogy: House keys: the owner, the household (group) and visitors (everyone else) can each look, change things, or go in and run things.

concepts.name: sudo
concepts.definition: Runs one command as the superuser (root), who can do anything to any file. Needed to install software, not for your own files.
concepts.analogy: The building manager's master key.

concepts.name: Process
concepts.definition: A program while it runs, with its own PID. Stopped with Ctrl+C or kill.
concepts.analogy: A recipe (the program) and the meal being cooked (the process).

concepts.name: Port
concepts.definition: A number from 0 to 65535 that picks which program on a computer gets a connection. Only one program can listen on a port at a time.
concepts.analogy: The apartment number; the IP address is the building's street address.

concepts.name: localhost
concepts.definition: The address 127.0.0.1: this computer. Requests to it never leave the machine.

concepts.name: Environment variable
concepts.definition: A named value a process gets a copy of when it starts; only exported ones reach programs. Used for settings and secrets. Always a string.
concepts.analogy: Sticky notes on the fridge that anything started from this terminal can read (the ones put up with export).

concepts.name: PATH
concepts.definition: The list of folders the shell searches, in order, for a command; "command not found" means none has it.
concepts.analogy: The drawers you check, in order, when you're looking for the scissors.

concepts.name: Standard streams
concepts.definition: stdin (input), stdout (normal output) and stderr (errors and messages), which every process has.

concepts.name: Redirection
concepts.definition: Sending a stream to a file instead of the screen: > replaces, >> appends, 2> sends stderr, 2>&1 sends both.

concepts.name: Pipe
concepts.definition: | sends one command's stdout into the next command's stdin, so small tools chain together.
concepts.analogy: A car wash: each station does one job and passes the car on.

concepts.name: Virtual environment
concepts.definition: A per-project folder (.venv) with the project's own packages and a link to its Python. Never committed.
concepts.analogy: Each project's own pantry, so two recipes never fight over ingredients.

concepts.name: Package manager
concepts.definition: A tool that downloads and installs packages from PyPI, like pip or uv.

concepts.name: Dependency
concepts.definition: A package a project needs. Dependencies have dependencies of their own.

concepts.name: pyproject.toml
concepts.definition: The file that describes a Python project: name, version, required Python, and dependency rules like httpx>=0.28.1.
concepts.analogy: A recipe's ingredient list ("flour, at least 500 g").

concepts.name: Lock file
concepts.definition: uv.lock: the exact version and hash of every package, dependencies of dependencies included. Written by uv, committed, never edited by hand.
concepts.analogy: The receipt: the exact brand and size bought, so the next cook buys exactly the same.

concepts.name: Semantic versioning
concepts.definition: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH version numbers: major can break things, minor adds features, patch fixes bugs. Not every package follows it (0.x, dates).
concepts.analogy: Phone software updates: 18 to 19 is a big update, 18.1 adds features, 18.1.1 only fixes bugs.

concepts.name: uv
concepts.definition: The tool backpy uses to manage Python versions, projects, environments and packages (init, add, run, sync).
